title: Bangers and Mash
subtitle: Pork sausages with creamy mashed potato and rich onion gravy
excerpt: Bangers and mash is one of the defining dishes of British pub cooking: fried or grilled pork sausages, smooth mashed potato, and a thick onion gravy. The sausages must be good quality; the mash must be properly buttered and warm; the gravy must be dark and well-seasoned. When all three are right, this is one of the most satisfying meals in the British repertoire.
sourceNotes: The term bangers comes from wartime sausages that contained water and would burst in the pan. The combination of sausages, mash, and onion gravy has been a British working-class staple since at least the early twentieth century.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the gravy a day ahead and reheat. Cook sausages and mash on the day.

content.text: Bangers and mash is a dish where quality of ingredients determines the result more than technique. A good quality pork sausage with a natural casing will colour and stay juicy; a poor sausage will split and leak. The onion gravy takes longer than the sausages; start it first, leave it to cook slowly, and it will look after itself.

items.prepNote: floury variety, peeled and cut into chunks

content.text: Melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a wide pan over low-medium heat. Add {{onion}} finely sliced onions and the thyme sprigs. Cook very slowly for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onions are golden, sweet, and collapsing. Do not rush this step.

Stir in {{plain-flour}} of flour and cook for 1 minute. Gradually pour in {{stock-beef}} of beef stock, stirring to prevent lumps. Add {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce. Simmer for 10 minutes until the gravy is thick and glossy. Season well.

While the gravy is simmering, boil {{potato}} of potato chunks in well-salted water until completely tender, about 18 minutes. Drain and steam dry for 2 minutes. Mash with {{unsalted-butter}} of butter and {{whole-milk}} of warm milk until smooth. Season well.
Cook {{sausages-pork}} pork sausages in a frying pan over medium heat for 15 to 18 minutes, turning every few minutes, until evenly browned on all sides and cooked through. Do not prick them.
Serve the sausages on the mash with the onion gravy spooned over generously.

items.cause: The heat was too high, building pressure inside before the skin could stretch.
items.fix: Cook sausages over medium, not high, heat. Do not prick them , the steam inside keeps them moist.

items.cause: Insufficient reduction, or the stock was too watery.
items.fix: Simmer uncovered until the gravy coats the back of a spoon. The onions will also thicken it as they break down further.

items.cause: The potato was over-worked after mashing, breaking down the starch into a paste.
items.fix: Mash minimally until smooth, then stop. Do not use a blender or food processor on mashed potato.

items.symptom: The onions are still sharp after 30 minutes
items.cause: The heat was too high and the onions coloured without caramelising properly.
items.fix: Cook the onions over the lowest heat you can maintain. They should wilt and turn golden gradually, not brown and crisp.

content.text: Bangers and mash has been a symbol of British pub food for generations, appearing on menus from the most basic roadside pub to gastro-pubs that charge accordingly. The name banger is widely believed to derive from wartime sausages with a high water content that would burst in the pan, though the term predates the war by some years. The onion gravy is the element that elevates it; without a good gravy, it is just sausages on potato.
